intro: Chopin’s Butterfly Étude packs its flight into little groups of four notes: a spring, then two clipped octaves. Edward Neeman plays this quick G♭-major study for Musopen.

sections.label: A · Springing octaves
sections.mNote: Four semiquavers to each beat, with sharply different touches

sections.label: B · Octaves over jumping bass
sections.mNote: The left hand jumps between bass notes and chords

sections.label: C · The four-note figure continues
sections.mNote: Slurred pairs and detached octaves keep changing places

sections.label: D · Last flights in G♭
sections.mNote: The right hand flies high above G♭-major chords

cues.title: Four notes, two touches
cues.text: Each beat has four semiquavers. The first two are joined under a slur; the next two are detached octaves. Underneath, the left hand jumps from a single bass note to a chord. Chopin marks the whole contraption leggiero — light.
cues.evidence: Breitkopf & Härtel first edition, opening bars: Allegro assai, leggiero, four-note right-hand groups and leaping left-hand quavers. Chopin Institute digital score: https://chopinscores.org/partytura/194
cues.how: Placed from the score; the timing is approximate.

cues.title: Neeman at the ballet
cues.text: Edward Neeman also works at the ballet piano. In 2014 he accompanies American Ballet Theatre on its Japanese tour. His other keyboard partnership is the Neeman Piano Duo, with his wife Stephanie.
cues.evidence: Australian National University biography of Edward Neeman documents the 2014 ballet tour and his duo with Stephanie Neeman: https://music.cass.anu.edu.au/people/dr-edward-neeman

composer.born: 1 March 1810 by his family’s reckoning; the parish register gives 22 February, Żelazowa Wola, Duchy of Warsaw
composer.epithet: He brought the opera singer’s breath and the mazurka’s wayward accents to a piano that could whisper across a room.
facts: Wojciech Żywny; composition with Józef Elsner in Warsaw, 1826–29
Warsaw · Paris from 1831 · summers at Nohant
Piano lessons, publishing and occasional concerts
The piano, from a few lines of mazurka to concertos and sonatas
composer.background:
In February 1832, a twenty-one-year-old Polish pianist played in the Pleyel rooms in Paris. Chopin had arrived the previous autumn, with two concertos behind him. The concert caught the attention of the city’s publishers; teaching soon supplied his living. He would spend the rest of his life in a profession that depended on people hearing him at close quarters. The great public virtuosos travelled from triumph to triumph. Chopin stayed in Paris and gave lessons.

He was born at Żelazowa Wola in 1810. His father, Nicolas, had come from France and worked as a tutor; his mother, Justyna Krzyżanowska, was Polish. They moved to Warsaw while Fryderyk was still a baby, when Nicolas obtained a teaching post at the Lyceum. At seven the boy already had a polonaise in print. Wojciech Żywny taught him the piano, with Bach and Mozart among his models; Józef Elsner later gave him a rigorous training in composition at Warsaw’s Main School of Music.
